sections.title: Embryology & Lung Development
sections.covers: Gestational stages and dating · fetal structures and how they change at birth · lung development stages · alveoli · surfactant · the amnion

q.q: What are the three prenatal stages, in order?
q.e: Ovum 12–14 days, embryo 54–56 days, then fetus 210–214 days — about 40 weeks in three trimesters.

q.q: About how long does the ovum stage last?
q.e: The ovum stage is 12–14 days; the embryo stage follows for 54–56 days.

q.q: The embryo stage ends when the embryo reaches what crown–rump length?
q.e: The embryo stage lasts 54–56 days and ends at about 3 cm crown–rump length; the fetal stage follows.

q.q: How long is the fetal stage?
q.e: Fetus = 210–214 days, the longest of the three prenatal stages.

q.q: A 3-week-old baby is classified as a(n):
q.e: Neonate = birth to 1 month · infant = 1 month to 1 year · child = over 1 year.

q.q: A 7-month-old is classified as a(n):
q.e: Infant = 1 month to 1 year.

q.q: A baby born at 35 weeks' gestation is:
o: Small for gestational age by definition
q.e: Term is >37 weeks; anything under 37 weeks is premature. SGA describes size, not dates.

q.q: Which formula is Nägele's rule for estimating the due date?
q.e: Nägele's rule: first day of the last menstrual period minus 3 months plus 7 days.

q.q: Quickening (first fetal movement felt by the mother) usually occurs at:
q.e: Quickening is felt at 16–22 weeks; fetal heart tones are heard at 16–20 weeks.

q.q: Which scoring systems estimate gestational age after birth?
q.e: Gestational age is scored with the Dubowitz or Ballard exam. APGAR rates the newborn's condition, not age.

q.q: A newborn whose weight falls below the 10th percentile for gestational age is:
q.e: AGA = 10th–90th percentile · SGA < 10th · LGA > 90th.

q.q: A newborn whose weight is above the 90th percentile for gestational age is:
q.e: LGA = above the 90th percentile.

q.q: By what week is the fetal heart fully formed?
q.e: The heart is fully formed by week 8 — the end of the embryo stage.

q.q: What is the fetal organ of respiration?
q.e: The placenta does gas exchange for the fetus; the fluid-filled lungs do not.

q.q: Which statement about maternal and fetal blood in the placenta is correct?
o: They mix freely in the villi
They mix only in the third trimester
They mix in the intervillous space
q.e: Exchange happens across membranes; maternal and fetal blood never mix.

q.q: How many vessels does a normal umbilical cord contain?
q.e: Two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein, cushioned in Wharton's jelly.

q.q: Which umbilical vessel carries oxygenated blood to the fetus?
q.e: The single umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus; the arteries return blood to the placenta.

q.q: Which fetal shunt lets blood bypass the liver?
q.e: Ductus venosus: umbilical vein → IVC, bypassing the liver.

q.q: Which fetal shunt connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta?
q.e: The ductus arteriosus sends blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the lungs.

q.q: At birth, why does systemic vascular resistance rise?
o: The placenta is removed from the circuit
q.e: Clamping the cord removes the low-resistance placenta, so SVR rises. Lung expansion and O₂ lower PVR.

q.q: At birth, why does pulmonary vascular resistance fall?
o: The lungs expand and oxygen dilates the vessels
The placenta is removed and stops absorbing blood
The foramen ovale closes and diverts flow away
Systemic pressure falls and pulls blood forward
q.e: Lung expansion and rising O₂ dilate the pulmonary vessels, so PVR falls.

q.q: Over about how long does the ductus arteriosus normally close after birth?
q.e: The DA closes over about 96 h; if it doesn't, surgery may be needed (PDA).

q.q: The ductus arteriosus becomes which remnant?
q.e: DA → ligamentum arteriosum · DV → ligamentum venosum · umbilical vein → ligamentum teres · umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments.

q.q: The umbilical vein becomes which remnant?
q.e: Umbilical vein → ligamentum teres.

q.q: The ductus venosus becomes which remnant?
q.e: Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum.

q.q: At term, the placenta covers about what fraction of the uterus?
q.e: At term the placenta covers about ⅓ of the uterus and weighs about 1 lb.

q.q: What is the amnion?
o: The sac around the fetus that holds the amniotic fluid
The outer layer of the placenta
The tissue around the umbilical vessels
q.e: The amnion is the sac surrounding the fetus; it contains the amniotic fluid. It forms around day 7.

q.q: Which is a function of amniotic fluid?
o: Protects the fetus, allows movement and aids thermoregulation
Carries oxygen and nutrients directly to the fetal tissues
Produces surfactant that coats the developing alveoli
Filters fetal blood and removes carbon dioxide from it
q.e: Amniotic fluid protects, lets the fetus move and helps with temperature. Oxygen comes through the umbilical vein.

q.q: Amniotic fluid is sampled to assess fetal lung maturity using the:
q.e: The lecithin/sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio in amniotic fluid estimates lung maturity; 2:1 = mature.

q.q: What are the five stages of fetal lung development, in order?
q.e: Embryonal (to wk 7; Whitaker says 8) → pseudoglandular (7–16) → canalicular (17–26) → saccular (26–36) → alveolar.

q.q: When does the lung bud appear?
q.e: The lung bud appears on day 24, in the embryonal stage.

q.q: In which stage do the airways branch so the lung looks like a gland?
q.e: Pseudoglandular means 'like a gland' — airways branching at weeks 7–16.

q.q: In which stage do bronchioles multiply, vessels form and alveoli begin?
q.e: Canalicular, weeks 17–26: vessels form, so gas exchange becomes possible at 24–25 weeks.

q.q: At about what gestational age does gas exchange first become possible?
q.e: Gas exchange is possible at 24–25 weeks, in the canalicular stage, once vessels have formed.

q.q: The saccular stage spans which weeks?
q.e: Saccular: weeks 26–36, when alveoli develop.

q.q: When do true alveoli appear?
q.e: True alveoli appear at 32–34 weeks, in the alveolar stage.

q.q: About how many alveoli does a term newborn have?
q.e: There are 50–150 million at birth; the adult has about 300 million.

q.q: Alveoli continue to increase in number until about what age?
q.e: Alveolar number keeps increasing until about age 8.

q.q: Which cells produce surfactant?
q.e: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant; type I cells form the gas-exchange surface.

q.q: What is the main phospholipid in surfactant?
q.e: Surfactant is mainly phospholipid — chiefly DPPC (lecithin) — plus neutral lipids and proteins.

q.q: Surfactant production begins at about:
q.e: Production starts at 24 weeks and is mature at about 35 weeks.

q.q: Surfactant is considered mature at about 35 weeks, when the L/S ratio is:
q.e: An L/S ratio of 2:1 indicates mature lungs.

q.q: What does surfactant do?
o: Lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open
Raises surface tension to stabilize alveoli
q.e: Lower surface tension keeps small alveoli from collapsing (Laplace) and reduces the work of breathing.

q.q: Surfactant deficiency causes which disease?
q.e: Respiratory distress syndrome is surfactant deficiency, mostly in preterm infants.

q.q: How is replacement surfactant given?
q.e: Exogenous surfactant is instilled into the ETT, either prophylactically or as rescue therapy.

q.q: Fetal lung fluid that isn't cleared at birth causes:
q.e: Retained lung fluid = transient tachypnea of the newborn — common after cesarean delivery.

sections.title: Fetal Circulation & Vessels
sections.covers: Fetal circulation pathway · foramen ovale · umbilical vessels · Wharton's jelly · arteries, pre- vs postductal sites and defects

q.q: The foramen ovale shunts blood from:
q.e: In the fetus the FO sends blood RA → LA, bypassing the lungs.

q.q: Why does blood cross the foramen ovale in the fetus?
o: Right-side pressures are higher than left
Left-side pressures are higher than right
q.e: Fluid-filled lungs resist flow, so fetal right-side pressure exceeds left and blood crosses RA → LA.

q.q: What closes the foramen ovale at birth?
o: Left-atrial pressure rising above right-atrial pressure
Right-atrial pressure rising above left-atrial pressure
Prostaglandin release from the expanding lungs
A drop in systemic pressure after cord clamping
q.e: Systemic pressure rises and PVR falls, so LA pressure exceeds RA and pushes the flap shut.

q.q: Failure of the foramen ovale to close results in:
q.e: A persistent opening between the atria is an ASD.

q.q: The umbilical arteries carry blood:
o: From the fetus back to the placenta
From the placenta to the fetus
From the RA to the LA
From the IVC to the liver
q.e: The two umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta; the single vein brings oxygenated blood in.

q.q: In a neonatal emergency, which umbilical vessel is used for drugs and fluids?
q.e: Vein = emergency drug and fluid access · artery = blood sampling and UAC.

q.q: Which umbilical vessel is used for an arterial line (UAC) and blood-gas sampling?
q.e: The umbilical artery catheter (UAC) is the preferred neonatal ABG site.

q.q: What is the most common complication of a UAC?
q.e: Thrombosis is the most common UAC complication.

q.q: After birth, the umbilical arteries become the:
q.e: Umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments; umbilical vein → ligamentum teres.

q.q: What is Wharton's jelly?
o: Gelatinous tissue surrounding the umbilical vessels
The fluid held inside the amniotic sac
The spongy inner lining of the placenta
A protective coating on the fetal skin
q.e: Wharton's jelly is the tough, gelatinous tissue around the three cord vessels.

q.q: What is the main function of Wharton's jelly?
o: Protects the vessels and keeps the cord from kinking
Carries oxygen from the placenta to the fetus
Produces amniotic fluid around the fetus
Filters maternal antibodies out of fetal blood
q.e: It insulates and protects the vessels and keeps the cord from kinking and cutting off flow.

q.q: After delivery, Wharton's jelly collapses the cord vessels within about:
q.e: The temperature change after delivery makes it collapse the vessels within about 5 minutes.

q.q: What triggers Wharton's jelly to collapse the umbilical vessels after delivery?
q.e: Cooling after delivery causes it to swell and clamp the vessels. Note: Wharton's jelly is not on the slides (Whitaker p. 9).

q.q: Which of these is a preductal site for sampling or SpO₂?
q.e: The right arm comes off the aorta before the ductus, so it is preductal; the UAC is postductal.

q.q: A UAC sample is considered:
q.e: The UAC sits in the descending aorta below the ductus — postductal.

q.q: The carotid and aortic bodies are:
q.e: The carotid and aortic bodies are chemoreceptors; baroreceptors sit at the carotid bifurcation and aortic arch.

q.q: Weak femoral pulses with strong arm pulses suggest:
q.e: Coarctation narrows the aorta, reducing flow to the lower body.

q.q: Which defect involves pulmonary artery obstruction?
q.e: Tetralogy includes pulmonary stenosis (pulmonary artery obstruction).

q.q: A single great vessel leaving both ventricles describes:
q.e: Truncus arteriosus = one common arterial trunk instead of a separate aorta and pulmonary artery.

q.q: Why are fetal right-side pressures higher than left?
o: Fluid-filled lungs resist flow while the placenta does not
The right ventricle is much thicker than the left
The foramen ovale stays closed until late gestation
Systemic resistance from the placenta is very high
q.e: High PVR from fluid-filled lungs plus low-resistance placenta reverse the normal pressures.

q.q: Oxygenated blood from the placenta first travels through the:
q.e: Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus → IVC → right atrium.

q.q: After the ductus venosus, oxygenated blood enters the:
q.e: DV → IVC → right atrium, then mostly across the foramen ovale.

q.q: Most blood entering the fetal right atrium from the IVC goes next to the:
o: Left atrium, through the foramen ovale
q.e: It crosses the foramen ovale to the left heart and out the aorta.

q.q: Blood the fetal right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary artery mostly goes:
o: Through the ductus arteriosus to the aorta
Into the lungs for gas exchange
q.e: RV → pulmonary artery → ductus arteriosus → aorta, bypassing the high-resistance lungs.

q.q: Correct order of fetal blood flow:
o: Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus → IVC → RA → foramen ovale → LA
Placenta → umbilical artery → ductus arteriosus → RA → LA
Placenta → umbilical vein → liver → SVC → RV → lungs
Placenta → ductus venosus → umbilical vein → aorta → LA
q.e: Vein → DV → IVC → RA → FO → left heart → aorta; the umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

q.q: If the fetal shunts fail to close after birth and pulmonary pressure stays high, the result is:
q.e: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn = persistent fetal circulation.

q.q: Which change happens at birth?
o: Systemic pressure rises and PVR falls
Systemic pressure falls and PVR rises
Both systemic pressure and PVR rise
q.e: Losing the placenta raises SVR; lung expansion and O₂ lower PVR.

sections.title: Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
sections.covers: Tocolytics and beta-sympathomimetics · chorioamnionitis · cervical dilation and stages of labor · placenta previa · indications for cesarean section

q.q: What is tocolysis?
q.e: Tocolysis = stopping premature labor, which affects about 12% of pregnancies.

q.q: Tocolytics are used before what gestational age?
q.e: Tocolysis is used before 37 weeks (premature labor), and also with placenta previa.

q.q: Which two drugs are beta-sympathomimetic tocolytics?
q.e: Terbutaline and ritodrine stimulate β-receptors to relax uterine muscle.

q.q: How do beta-sympathomimetics stop preterm labor?
o: Stimulate β-receptors to relax uterine smooth muscle
Block calcium channels in the uterus
q.e: β-stimulation relaxes uterine smooth muscle.

q.q: A mother on terbutaline develops tachycardia and shortness of breath. Which side effect is most concerning?
q.e: β-agonist side effects: maternal tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema.

q.q: Which maternal lab change is expected with β-agonist tocolytics?
q.e: β-agonists raise glucose and drive potassium into cells.

q.q: A newborn whose mother received β-agonist tocolytics should be watched for:
q.e: Fetal hyperglycemia triggers insulin; after birth the glucose supply stops, causing rebound hypoglycemia.

q.q: A newborn is hypotonic and apneic after the mother received a tocolytic. Which drug is most likely?
q.e: Magnesium lowers muscle contractility; hypermagnesemia makes the newborn floppy and apneic.

q.q: Which tocolytic can constrict the fetal ductus arteriosus?
q.e: Indomethacin blocks prostaglandins, which keep the ductus open.

q.q: Nifedipine works as a tocolytic by:
q.e: Nifedipine is a calcium-channel blocker.

q.q: What is chorioamnionitis?
o: Infection of the fetal membranes and amniotic fluid
Inflammation of the uterine lining after delivery
q.e: Bacterial infection and inflammation of the membranes and amniotic fluid.

q.q: Chorioamnionitis risk rises most when membranes have been ruptured longer than:
q.e: Organisms ascend the birth canal; rupture >24 h greatly raises the risk.

q.q: What classic clue suggests chorioamnionitis at delivery?
q.e: Foul-smelling fluid and baby. Green staining suggests meconium.

q.q: A newborn exposed to chorioamnionitis is at increased risk of:
q.e: Infected fluid raises the risk of neonatal sepsis and pneumonia.

q.q: How is the newborn treated after chorioamnionitis?
q.e: Treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin).

q.q: At what dilation is the cervix fully dilated?
q.e: Full dilation = 10 cm.

q.q: Cervical effacement refers to:
o: Thinning of the cervix, measured in percent
Widening of the cervix, measured in cm
q.e: Effacement = thinning (%); dilation = widening (cm).

q.q: Stage 1 of labor runs from:
o: Onset of contractions to full dilation
Full dilation to delivery of the baby
Delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta
q.e: Stage 1: contractions → full (10 cm) dilation.

q.q: Stage 2 of labor runs from:
o: Full dilation to delivery of the baby
Onset of contractions to full dilation
Delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta
Rupture of membranes to full dilation
q.e: Stage 2: full dilation → delivery.

q.q: Stage 3 of labor is:
q.e: Stage 3 ends with delivery of the placenta.

q.q: Placenta previa is a placenta that:
o: Implants low, near or over the cervical opening
Separates early from the uterine wall
Is too small for gestational age
q.e: Previa = low implantation near or over the os. Early separation is abruptio placentae.

q.q: A placenta that completely covers the cervical os is:
q.e: Types: low (marginal) · partial · total (completely covers the os).

q.q: How is placenta previa diagnosed?
q.e: Placenta previa is diagnosed by ultrasound.

q.q: Why is placenta previa dangerous for the fetus?
o: It blocks fetal passage and can cause asphyxia
It causes the ductus to close early
q.e: It blocks the birth canal, risks abruption and is a cause of fetal asphyxia — a high-risk pregnancy.

q.q: Which is a common indication for cesarean section?
q.e: Indications: prior cesarean, dystocia, breech, fetal distress; also transverse lie, abruption, active herpes.

q.q: Dystocia, an indication for cesarean, means:
q.e: Dystocia = difficult labor that fails to progress.

q.q: A mother with active genital herpes lesions should deliver by:
q.e: Cesarean avoids passing the baby through infected lesions (HSV-2).

q.q: After a cesarean birth, which newborn problem is more likely?
q.e: Without the squeeze of the birth canal, lung fluid is retained → TTN.

sections.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
sections.covers: Fetal asphyxia — presentation and treatment · primary vs secondary apnea · APGAR score · meconium aspiration · indications for PPV · intubation

q.q: Asphyxia is the combination of:
q.e: Asphyxia = hypoxia + hypercapnia + acidosis.

q.q: Which is a cause of fetal asphyxia?
q.e: Causes: maternal hypoxia, poor placental flow, cord blockage, fetal anemia or drugs.

q.q: Fetal bradycardia is defined as a fetal heart rate below:
q.e: Fetal bradycardia <100 bpm, often from asphyxia. Normal is 120–160.

q.q: Which fetal monitoring finding suggests asphyxia?
q.e: Asphyxia signs: bradycardia, loss of variability, late decelerations, meconium-stained fluid, low scalp pH.

q.q: A fetal scalp pH of 7.15 indicates:
q.e: Scalp pH >7.25 normal · 7.20–7.24 slight · <7.20 severe asphyxia.

q.q: The fetal heart tracing suggests umbilical cord compression. What is a first step before delivery?
o: Reposition the mother and give her O₂
q.e: Before birth: O₂ to the mother, reposition her (for cord compression), amnioinfusion, then rapid delivery if needed.

q.q: Treatment of asphyxia after birth aims for:
o: Immediate reversal of hypoxia and acidosis
q.e: Warm, dry, open the airway, ventilate — reverse hypoxia and acidosis immediately.

q.q: As asphyxia progresses, the newborn's heart rate and blood pressure:
q.e: HR and BP fall as asphyxia worsens; breathing goes from primary apnea to gasping to secondary apnea.

q.q: An apneic newborn's HR is 50 after 30 seconds of effective PPV. Next step?
q.e: HR <60 after 30 s of PPV → add compressions, 3 compressions : 1 breath.

q.q: What is the neonatal compression-to-ventilation ratio?
q.e: Neonatal: 3 compressions to 1 breath.

q.q: Neonatal epinephrine for resuscitation is given as:
q.e: Epinephrine 1:10,000, 0.1–0.3 mL/kg IV.

q.q: Volume expansion for a newborn with blood loss is:
q.e: Volume 10 mL/kg for blood loss.

q.q: The first steps of newborn resuscitation are:
o: Warm, dry and open the airway
q.e: Warm, dry, position and clear the airway, then assess breathing and heart rate.

q.q: What is the sequence of breathing during asphyxia?
o: Primary apnea → weak gasping → secondary apnea
q.e: Primary apnea, then weak gasps, then complete cessation (secondary apnea). Watch: the slide labels the gasping itself as secondary apnea; Whitaker puts gasping just before it.

q.q: Which statement about secondary apnea is correct?
o: Breathing will not return without PPV
q.e: In secondary apnea stimulation doesn't work; only PPV restores breathing.

q.q: A newborn is born apneic. You can't tell if it is primary or secondary apnea. You should:
o: Treat it as secondary apnea and ventilate
Wait for the 1-minute APGAR before acting
Give naloxone first, then reassess breathing
q.e: Treat every apneic newborn as if in secondary apnea: ventilate.

q.q: During secondary apnea, heart rate and blood pressure:
q.e: HR and BP keep falling until PPV is given.

q.q: How many signs does the APGAR score assess?
q.e: Five signs (heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, color), each 0/1/2.

q.q: When is the APGAR score routinely taken?
q.e: At 1 and 5 minutes; repeated every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes if low.

q.q: A heart rate of 90 earns how many APGAR points?
A baby with a pink body and blue hands and feet scores what for color?
q.e: Acrocyanosis = 1. All pink = 2; pale/blue = 0.

q.q: A baby who grimaces when stimulated scores what for reflex irritability?
q.e: Reflex irritability: 0 none · 1 grimace · 2 crying.

q.q: A newborn with irregular, gasping breaths scores what for respiratory effort?
q.e: Respiratory effort: 0 apnea · 1 irregular/gasping · 2 crying.

q.q: At 1 minute: HR 80, gasping, some flexion, grimace, blue extremities with pink body. APGAR?
q.e: HR 1 + effort 1 + tone 1 + reflex 1 + color 1 = 5.

q.q: At 5 minutes: HR 140, crying, well flexed, crying to stimulus, acrocyanosis. APGAR?
q.e: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 (acrocyanosis) = 9.

q.q: Which APGAR score has the most value for predicting future impairment?
q.e: The 5-minute score predicts future impairment; the 1-minute score reflects immediate condition.

q.q: Which APGAR scores call for intervention?
o: Below 6 at 1 minute or below 7 at 5 minutes
Below 8 at 1 minute or below 9 at 5 minutes
q.e: <6 at 1 min or <7 at 5 min needs intervention.

q.q: A newborn is apneic at birth. When should you calculate the APGAR before acting?
o: Never delay resuscitation to score it
q.e: Start resuscitation immediately; never delay it to score the APGAR.

q.q: Why does a fetus pass meconium in utero?
o: Asphyxia increases gut movement and relaxes the anal sphincter
Infection of the amniotic fluid causes fetal diarrhea
Prematurity leaves the anal sphincter weak and open
Maternal β-agonist tocolytics stimulate the fetal gut
q.e: Asphyxia triggers gut movement and sphincter relaxation; the fetus then gasps meconium in.

q.q: Meconium aspiration syndrome mostly affects which babies?
q.e: Preterm guts rarely pass meconium; MAS is a term/post-term disease.

q.q: Meconium causes air trapping in the lungs through a:
q.e: Partial obstruction lets air in but not out — ball-valve air trapping that can lead to air leaks.

q.q: Which complications does meconium aspiration cause?
o: Air leaks, chemical pneumonitis and PPHN
ROP, NEC and kernicterus in the newborn
q.e: Ball-valve air trapping (air leaks), chemical pneumonitis, and PPHN.

q.q: What does the chest x-ray typically show in MAS?
o: Clear lungs with a small heart
q.e: MAS CXR: patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation. Ground-glass with low volumes is RDS.

q.q: A baby is born through meconium-stained fluid with HR 80, weak effort and poor tone. Next step?
o: Bulb-suction the mouth and nose only
q.e: Not vigorous (HR <100, weak effort, poor tone) → intubate and suction the trachea, per the deck. Current NRP no longer suctions the trachea routinely — expect that answer on the NBRC.

q.q: A baby born through meconium is crying with good tone and HR 150. What should you do?
q.e: A vigorous baby gets bulb suction of the mouth and nose only.

q.q: Amnioinfusion before delivery helps in MAS by:
o: Diluting the meconium with warm saline
Stopping labor so the fetus can recover
Maturing the fetal lungs before delivery
Closing the ductus before the first breath
q.e: Warm saline is infused into the uterus to dilute thick meconium.

q.q: Ventilator strategy for MAS with air trapping includes:
o: PEEP and a long expiratory time
Short expiratory time and high rate
q.e: Long Te lets trapped air out; PEEP helps keep airways open. Add surfactant, and iNO if PPHN develops.

q.q: Which is an indication for positive-pressure ventilation in a newborn?
q.e: PPV for apnea, gasping, or HR <100 despite spontaneous breathing.

q.q: What rate is used for neonatal PPV?
q.e: Give 40–60 breaths/min and reassess at 30 s.

q.q: After 30 seconds of PPV, the HR is 80. What next?
q.e: HR 60–100 → continue PPV. HR <60 → add compressions.

q.q: When do you reassess the heart rate after starting PPV?
q.e: Reassess after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

q.q: What is the standard neonatal intubation route?
o: Oral, with a straight blade and uncuffed tube
Nasal, with a curved blade and cuffed tube
Oral, with a curved blade and cuffed tube
q.e: Orotracheal with a Miller (straight) blade and an uncuffed tube.

q.q: Which Miller blade size is used for a term newborn?
q.e: Size 0 for preterm, size 1 for term.

q.q: Which is an indication for neonatal intubation?
q.e: Indications: non-vigorous meconium, ineffective bag-mask, prolonged PPV, compressions, surfactant, diaphragmatic hernia.

q.q: How long should each neonatal intubation attempt last?
q.e: Limit each attempt to 30 s.

q.q: How is neonatal ETT placement confirmed?
o: Bilateral breath sounds, CO₂ detector and CXR
Pulse oximetry alone, once SpO₂ reaches 90%
Gastric sounds heard over the stomach
Rising APGAR score at the next check
q.e: Confirm with breath sounds, an exhaled CO₂ detector and chest x-ray.

sections.covers: Increased work of breathing · the physical exam and distress signs · normal HR and RR · bradycardia and tachycardia · the infant larynx · cyanosis · chest x-ray uses

q.q: A newborn's RR above what value is tachypnea?
q.e: Newborn RR 30–60; above 60 = tachypnea, an RDS sign.

q.q: What is grunting?
o: Exhaling against a partly closed glottis
Inward pulling of the chest wall
q.e: Grunting = closing the glottis on exhalation, creating back-pressure.

q.q: Why does an infant grunt?
o: To create its own PEEP and keep alveoli open
q.e: Grunting is self-made PEEP; it signals low lung volume and tries to raise FRC.

q.q: Grunting tells you the infant's lung volume (FRC) is:
q.e: Grunting is an attempt to raise a low FRC. Note: the RDS slide says 'increased FRC' — RDS actually lowers FRC.

q.q: What causes retractions in a newborn?
o: Stiff lungs pulling the soft chest wall inward
q.e: Low-compliance lungs plus a cartilaginous chest wall → the chest is sucked in on inspiration.

q.q: Retractions are described by location as:
q.e: Retractions are intercostal, substernal or suprasternal, graded mild to severe.

q.q: What does nasal flaring accomplish?
o: Widens the nares to lower airway resistance
Warms and humidifies the inspired air
Narrows the nares to slow expiratory flow
q.e: Nasal flaring widens the nares to cut resistance and bring in more air.

q.q: In RDS, what happens to FRC?
q.e: Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse, lowering FRC. Watch: the slide says 'increased FRC' — a slide error.

q.q: Which is a cause of increased work of breathing in a newborn?
q.e: Causes: RDS, TTN, pneumothorax and air leaks, pneumonia, MAS.

q.q: Which infant feature predisposes to respiratory distress?
q.e: Narrow airway, cartilaginous chest wall, low reserve and high metabolic rate.

q.q: What is the first step in the neonatal exam?
q.e: Order: observe → history and gestational age → AGA/SGA/LGA → quiet exam → hands-on → reflexes.

q.q: Which reflexes are checked at the end of the neonatal exam?
o: Doll's eyes, cough, gag and blink
q.e: Newborn reflexes: rooting, suck, grasp, Moro.

q.q: Normal axillary temperature for a newborn is:
q.e: Normal temp 36.2–37.3 °C axillary.

q.q: Neonatal apnea is a pause in breathing longer than:
o: 15–20 seconds, or shorter with cyanosis or bradycardia
5 seconds, whether or not the color changes
60 seconds, as long as the heart rate stays normal
2 minutes, or any pause during feeding
q.e: Apnea = >15–20 s, or any pause with cyanosis or bradycardia.

q.q: A newborn has a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen and respiratory distress. Suspect:
q.e: Abdominal contents are in the chest, leaving the abdomen sunken.

q.q: A shifted point of maximal impulse (PMI) suggests:
q.e: Air or volume loss shifts the mediastinum and the PMI.

q.q: Weak femoral pulses in a newborn suggest:
q.e: Coarctation narrows the aorta and reduces flow to the legs.

q.q: A bulging fontanelle indicates:
q.e: A bulging fontanelle means raised ICP; a sunken one suggests dehydration.

q.q: What is the first treatment for a newborn in respiratory distress?
q.e: O₂ first, then CPAP or ventilation as needed.

q.q: In a child over 1 year, a resting RR above what needs investigation?
q.e: After age 1, resting RR >40 needs investigation; after age 5, >35.

q.q: Treatment for TTN is:
q.e: TTN = O₂, CPAP. RDS = steroids, surfactant, ventilation.

q.q: Treatment for croup includes:
q.e: Croup = humidity, fluids, observation. Epiglottitis = O₂, prepare to intubate.

q.q: For the pediatric lung exam, what helps localize the disease?
o: An ABG drawn from the radial artery
Heart rate and blood pressure trends
q.e: Localize: auscultate, percuss, CXR. Gas exchange: ABG, SpO₂.

q.q: Normal newborn heart rate is:
q.e: Newborn and fetus: 120–160 bpm.

q.q: Approximate normal heart rate of a 10-year-old?
q.e: About 80 at 5 years, 70 at 10 years, 60s by 15 years.

q.q: In newborn resuscitation, HR below what value calls for PPV?
q.e: >100 is the goal · <100 → PPV · <60 → compressions.

q.q: In newborn resuscitation, HR below what value calls for compressions?
q.e: HR <60 after 30 s of effective PPV → compressions.

q.q: Normal newborn respiratory rate is:
q.e: Newborn RR 30–60.

q.q: Approximate RR of a 5-year-old?
q.e: Infant about 30, 5 years about 22, 10–15 years 18–19.

q.q: In a child over 5, a resting RR above what needs investigation?
q.e: After age 5, resting RR >35 needs investigation.

q.q: Newborn bradycardia is a heart rate below:
q.e: Fetal and newborn bradycardia: <100 bpm.

q.q: For a 6-year-old, bradycardia is a heart rate below:
q.e: Children: <100 under 3 years · <60 at 3–9 years · <50 at 9–16 years.

q.q: Bradycardia in a child most often means:
q.e: Pediatric bradycardia is usually hypoxic; fix oxygenation and ventilation first.

q.q: A child has HR 50 with poor perfusion despite ventilation and O₂. Next step?
q.e: HR <60 with poor perfusion → CPR.

q.q: Fetal tachycardia is a heart rate above:
q.e: Fetal tachycardia >180 bpm (the deck's cutoff).

q.q: The most common cause of fetal tachycardia is:
q.e: Maternal fever is most common; β-agonist tocolytics also cause it.

q.q: Newborn tachycardia is a heart rate above:
q.e: Newborn tachycardia >160 bpm.

q.q: Pediatric tachycardia is first classified by:
q.e: Narrow QRS = sinus or SVT; wide QRS is treated differently.

q.q: A stable child with SVT should first receive:
q.e: SVT: vagal maneuvers → adenosine → cardioversion if unstable.

q.q: If vagal maneuvers fail in a stable child with SVT, give:
q.e: Adenosine follows vagal maneuvers; cardiovert if unstable.

q.q: Compared with an adult, the infant larynx is:
q.e: The infant larynx sits higher and more anterior than the adult's.

q.q: The narrowest part of the infant airway is the:
q.e: Narrowest at the cricoid, so a little swelling causes major obstruction.

q.q: The infant epiglottis is:
q.e: Large, floppy, U-shaped — easier to lift with a straight blade.

q.q: Why are a straight blade and uncuffed tube used in infants?
o: High anterior larynx, floppy epiglottis and narrow cricoid
Low posterior larynx and a short, stiff epiglottis
Narrowest point at the cords, so cuffs damage them
Cuffed tubes are not made in infant sizes at all
q.e: The straight Miller blade lifts the floppy epiglottis; the narrow cricoid seals around an uncuffed tube.

q.q: Cyanosis appears when desaturated hemoglobin reaches about:
q.e: About 5 g/dL of desaturated Hb — so hypoxemia may already be significant.

q.q: Where should you check for central cyanosis?
q.e: Check central color on the trunk; in dark skin, check the mucous membranes.

q.q: Blue hands and feet with a pink body right after birth is:
q.e: Acrocyanosis is normal after birth.

q.q: Central cyanosis doesn't improve on 100% O₂. What should you suspect?
o: A right-to-left shunt (PPHN or heart disease)
Hypothermia from a cold delivery room
q.e: Failure to correct with 100% O₂ suggests a right-to-left shunt.

q.q: Which condition commonly causes cyanosis in the newborn?
q.e: Cyanosis is seen in PPHN, pneumothorax, apnea and Wilson-Mikity.

q.q: Where should a neonatal ETT tip sit on CXR?
o: Halfway between the carina and the clavicles
Down in the right mainstem bronchus
q.e: ETT tip midway between the carina and the clavicles.

q.q: Which is a use of the CXR in neonates and children?
q.e: Confirm diagnosis, check tubes and lines, follow progression.

q.q: A CXR is useful to identify which of the following?
q.e: Specific uses: BPD, pneumomediastinum, pneumopericardium, foreign body.

sections.title: Thermoregulation & Fluids
sections.covers: Thermoregulation methods and why RTs care · the neutral thermal environment · four routes of heat loss · cold stress and its consequences · insensible water loss

q.q: Thermoregulation is the balance between:
q.e: Thermoregulation = balancing heat production against heat loss.

q.q: Newborns produce heat mainly by:
q.e: Newborns can't shiver well; they rely on brown fat (nonshivering thermogenesis).

q.q: The neutral thermal environment is the temperature at which the baby has the:
q.e: NTE = the temperature range with the lowest O₂ consumption.

q.q: Target rectal temperature for a newborn is:
q.e: Goal rectal temperature 36.5–37.5 °C.

q.q: Which route of heat loss is usually the largest in the newborn?
q.e: Radiant loss is largest — heat radiating to cooler surrounding surfaces.

q.q: A wet newborn loses heat by evaporation. The fix is to:
q.e: Evaporative loss → dry immediately.

q.q: A newborn placed on a cold scale loses heat by:
q.e: Conduction = direct contact with a cooler surface. Fix: warm mattress and surfaces.

q.q: Heat lost to drafts or cool moving air is:
q.e: Convection = moving air. Avoid drafts and warm the gases.

q.q: Heat lost to cool walls and windows nearby, without contact, is:
q.e: Radiant loss → cap, warm blanket, radiant warmer.

q.q: Blowing cold O₂ across a newborn's face causes heat loss mainly by:
q.e: Moving cold gas = convective loss; warm the gases.

q.q: Advantage of an incubator over a radiant warmer?
o: Easier hands-on access to the baby
Lets staff reach the baby more easily
q.e: Incubator = controlled and quiet but limits access.

q.q: Disadvantage of a radiant warmer?
o: Harder to control temperature and more water loss
Very limited access to the baby during care
Too quiet to hear alarms from the bedside
Cannot be used during newborn resuscitation
q.e: Radiant warmer = good access, but harder to control and more insensible water loss.

q.q: In pediatric patients, hypothermia most often follows:
q.e: Pediatric hypothermia mostly follows trauma; CNS injury can stop shivering. Prevent it in burns.

q.q: Why does thermoregulation matter to the RT?
o: Cold causes acidosis, pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypoxemia
Cold boosts surfactant production and lung compliance
Cold lowers O₂ consumption and protects the brain
Cold stimulates breathing and prevents newborn apnea
q.e: Cold → acidosis → pulmonary vasoconstriction → hypoxemia.

q.q: Cold stress is defined as:
o: Any drop below the thermoneutral temperature
q.e: Cold stress = any drop below the thermoneutral temperature.

q.q: Which hormone triggers brown-fat burning during cold stress?
q.e: Norepinephrine → brown fat → heat (nonshivering thermogenesis).

q.q: Burning brown fat during cold stress causes:
o: Increased O₂ consumption and decreased glucose
Decreased O₂ consumption and increased glucose
Increased glucose with no change in O₂ use
Decreased heart rate with lower O₂ demand
q.e: Thermogenesis raises O₂ use and burns glucose.

q.q: Correct cold-stress chain:
o: Vasoconstriction → anaerobic metabolism → metabolic acidosis → pulmonary vasoconstriction → hypoxemia
Vasodilation → aerobic metabolism → respiratory alkalosis → pulmonary vasodilation → hyperoxemia
Shivering → hyperglycemia → respiratory alkalosis → pulmonary vasodilation → normal PaO₂
Vasoconstriction → aerobic metabolism → metabolic alkalosis → pulmonary vasodilation → hyperoxemia
q.e: Peripheral vasoconstriction → anaerobic metabolism → metabolic acidosis → pulmonary vasoconstriction → hypoxemia → death if uncorrected.

q.q: Cold stress causes what acid-base disturbance?
q.e: Anaerobic metabolism produces lactic acid → metabolic acidosis.

q.q: A cold-stressed newborn becomes more hypoxemic because:
q.e: Acidosis and cold constrict the pulmonary vessels, raising PVR and shunt.

q.q: Which is a consequence of cold stress?
q.e: Hypoglycemia, lost calories for growth, less surfactant, bradycardia and arrhythmias.

q.q: Cold stress affects surfactant by:
q.e: Cold stress lowers surfactant production.

q.q: Insensible water loss is water lost by:
o: Evaporation from the skin and respiratory tract
Urine output measured by diaper weight
Stool and gastric losses after feeding
q.e: IWL = evaporative loss from skin and airways.

q.q: Why do premature infants have high insensible water loss?
q.e: Thin, permeable skin and small size increase IWL.

q.q: Which increases insensible water loss?
q.e: Radiant warmers and phototherapy raise IWL; humidity and heat shields lower it.

q.q: Which decreases insensible water loss?
q.e: Humidity and heat shields reduce evaporative loss.

q.q: Which raises insensible water loss in a newborn?
q.e: Respiratory distress, high temperature, skin breakdown, motor activity and crying all increase IWL.

q.q: Why do children dehydrate faster than adults?
o: Larger body surface area relative to size
Lower metabolic rate and less heat made
Thicker skin that holds in less water
Less total body water than adults
q.e: A proportionately larger BSA means more evaporative loss.

sections.title: Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
sections.covers: Retinopathy of prematurity · NEC · pneumothorax · ABG interpretation and RDS · PPHN and its treatment

q.q: Retinopathy of prematurity is caused by:
o: Cold stress in the delivery room
q.e: Immature retinal vessels plus high O₂.

q.q: Which infants are at highest risk for ROP?
o: Under 31 weeks and 1250 g or less
Infants of diabetic mothers at term
q.e: Highest risk: <31 weeks and ≤1250 g.

q.q: What is the first event in ROP when PaO₂ is high?
q.e: High PaO₂ → vasoconstriction → vessel necrosis → abnormal new vessels → scar → detachment.

q.q: ROP was formerly called:
q.e: ROP = the old term retrolental fibroplasia.

q.q: ROP stage 5 is:
q.e: 1 line · 2 ridge · 3 fibrovascular proliferation · 4 partial detachment · 5 total detachment.

q.q: A demarcation line on exam indicates ROP stage:
q.e: Stage 1 = demarcation line; stage 2 = ridge.

q.q: Treatment of ROP includes:
q.e: Cryotherapy or laser; vitrectomy/lensectomy for late stages.

q.q: Target PaO₂ to help prevent ROP is:
q.e: Careful O₂ use with monitoring, PaO₂ 50–70.

q.q: NEC is:
o: Ischemia and necrosis of the intestine
q.e: Necrotizing enterocolitis = ischemic, necrotic bowel, mostly in premature, formula-fed babies.

q.q: What three factors combine to cause NEC?
o: Bowel wall ischemia, bacterial invasion and formula feeding
Hyperoxia, prematurity and long phototherapy sessions
Cold stress, hypoglycemia and metabolic acidosis
q.e: (1) ischemia (asphyxia, PDA, UAC, exchange transfusion), (2) bacteria, (3) formula. Breast milk protects.

q.q: Which type of feeding protects against NEC?
q.e: Breast milk is protective.

q.q: Which sign suggests NEC?
q.e: Bloody (guaiac +) stools, distention, bilious residuals and vomiting, feeding intolerance.

q.q: What is the classic x-ray finding in NEC?
o: Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall)
Steeple sign on the AP neck film
Thumb sign on the lateral neck film
q.e: Pneumatosis intestinalis — gas in the bowel wall.

q.q: First-line treatment for NEC is:
o: Stop feeds, NG suction, IV nutrition and antibiotics
Larger feeds to rest the bowel faster
q.e: NPO, NG suction, IV nutrition, ampicillin + gentamicin, serial abdominal x-rays; surgery if perforated.

q.q: When is surgery needed for NEC?
q.e: Surgery is for perforation.

q.q: Most neonatal pneumothoraces result from:
q.e: Most come from ventilation; more common with RDS and MAS.

q.q: A ventilated newborn suddenly worsens with asymmetric chest rise and a shifted PMI. Suspect:
q.e: Sudden distress, asymmetric rise and shifted PMI = pneumothorax.

q.q: A bedside test for neonatal pneumothorax is:
q.e: Transillumination with a bright light — the affected side glows.

q.q: CXR in a tension pneumothorax shows:
o: Air without lung markings and the mediastinum shifted away
Ground-glass lungs with air bronchograms and low volumes
Patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation on both sides
Air without lung markings and the mediastinum shifted toward it
q.e: Air with no lung markings; tension shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side.

q.q: A newborn with a tension pneumothorax is crashing. Immediate treatment?
o: Chest tube placement in the OR
q.e: Emergency: needle aspiration; then a chest tube for an ongoing leak.

q.q: A small pneumothorax in a stable newborn may be managed by:
q.e: Observe if small; needle if emergency; chest tube if ongoing.

q.q: Chest tube suction for a neonatal pneumothorax is set at:
q.e: Suction −15 to −25 cm H₂O.

q.q: Late signs of an untreated pneumothorax include:
q.e: Distress progresses to bradycardia, cyanosis, apnea and hypotension.

q.q: Normal pH for neonates and children is:
q.e: Safe pH 7.35–7.45 (acceptable 7.30–7.50).

q.q: Target PaO₂ for a neonate is:
q.e: Neonate PaO₂ 50–70; child 80–100.

q.q: Normal PaCO₂ is:
q.e: PaCO₂ 35–45; HCO₃⁻ 22–26; BE ±4.

q.q: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 58, HCO₃⁻ 24. Interpretation?
q.e: Low pH with high PaCO₂ and normal HCO₃⁻ = acute (uncompensated) respiratory acidosis.

q.q: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 38, HCO₃⁻ 17. Interpretation?
q.e: Low pH with low HCO₃⁻ and normal PaCO₂ = metabolic acidosis.

q.q: pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 30, HCO₃⁻ 23. Interpretation?
q.e: High pH with low PaCO₂ = respiratory alkalosis.

q.q: pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 55, HCO₃⁻ 32. Interpretation?
q.e: Normal pH with high PaCO₂ and high HCO₃⁻ — the kidneys have compensated a respiratory acidosis.

q.q: The typical RDS blood-gas picture is:
o: Hypoxemia, rising PaCO₂ and mixed respiratory-metabolic acidosis
Hyperoxemia, falling PaCO₂ and pure respiratory alkalosis
Normal PaO₂, normal PaCO₂ and a metabolic alkalosis
Hypoxemia, falling PaCO₂ and a metabolic alkalosis
q.e: RDS: hypoxemia that responds poorly to O₂ + rising PaCO₂ + mixed (lactic) acidosis.

q.q: In RDS, why is there a metabolic component to the acidosis?
o: Hypoxemia causes lactic acid from anaerobic metabolism
The kidneys excrete too much bicarbonate
q.e: Tissue hypoxia → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid.

q.q: An RDS infant has PaCO₂ 65 and pH 7.20. What is indicated?
o: Continue the nasal cannula and recheck
Sodium bicarbonate with no other change
Observe and repeat the ABG in 6 hours
q.e: Intubate if PaCO₂ >60 with pH <7.25.

q.q: Acceptable RDS targets are PaO₂ 50–80, PaCO₂ under 60, and pH above:
q.e: RDS targets: PaO₂ 50–80, PaCO₂ <60, pH >7.25.

q.q: Preferred site for neonatal ABG sampling is:
q.e: UAC is preferred.

q.q: A capillary blood gas is reliable for:
o: pH and PaCO₂, but not PaO₂
PaO₂, but not pH or PaCO₂
q.e: Capillary samples are OK for pH and PaCO₂ but not PaO₂.

q.q: How long after a ventilator change should you draw a neonatal ABG?
q.e: Draw 15–30 min after vent changes.

q.q: PPHN is also called:
q.e: PPHN = persistent fetal circulation.

q.q: In PPHN, blood shunts right-to-left through the:
q.e: High pulmonary pressure pushes blood R → L across the FO and DA.

q.q: Which babies usually develop PPHN?
o: Term babies after asphyxia or MAS
q.e: Usually term; causes include asphyxia, MAS, sepsis, diaphragmatic hernia, cold, acidosis.

q.q: Which finding is typical of PPHN?
q.e: Blood shunted R → L through the DA lowers postductal oxygenation.

q.q: Which test helps diagnose PPHN?
q.e: Hyperoxia test, pre/postductal PaO₂, hyperoxia-hyperventilation test, echo.

q.q: Which therapy directly dilates the pulmonary vessels in PPHN?
q.e: iNO is a selective pulmonary vasodilator.

q.q: ECMO for PPHN is:
o: A last resort when other treatments fail
The first-line treatment for every case
Used only in very preterm infants
q.e: Normal temperature, fluids, glucose and BP; minimal handling; ventilation (HFV); iNO; ECMO last.

q.q: Why is minimal handling important in PPHN?
o: Handling raises the risk of NEC
Touch speeds closure of the ductus
q.e: Stress and agitation worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction and shunting.

sections.title: Persistent Illness & Infection
sections.covers: Bacterial infections of the neonate · hyperbilirubinemia · the TORCH infections · atrial septal defect

q.q: How do bacteria usually reach the fetus?
o: Ascending the birth canal after membranes rupture
Through the umbilical vein from the mother's lungs
Through the fetal skin in the first trimester
q.e: Organisms ascend after ROM, enter the fetal mouth, then lungs, gut and bloodstream.

q.q: The two main organisms in neonatal sepsis are:
o: Group B strep and E. coli
q.e: GBS and E. coli; also Listeria, Staph aureus, Klebsiella, H. influenzae.

q.q: Rupture of membranes longer than how long greatly raises infection risk?
q.e: >24 h greatly raises risk.

q.q: Which maternal condition greatly increases neonatal infection risk?
q.e: Chorioamnionitis greatly raises the risk.

q.q: A preterm septic newborn's temperature is most likely to be:
q.e: Temperature instability — preemies often become hypothermic rather than febrile.

q.q: Which WBC count suggests neonatal sepsis?
Which is a sign of neonatal sepsis?
q.e: Signs: respiratory distress, tachycardia, lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability.

q.q: How is neonatal sepsis diagnosed?
q.e: Culture confirms the organism.

q.q: Standard empiric treatment for neonatal sepsis is:
q.e: Broad-spectrum ampicillin + gentamicin.

q.q: When are mothers screened for group B strep?
q.e: GBS screening at 35–37 weeks.

q.q: Jaundice becomes visible when bilirubin exceeds about:
q.e: Jaundice shows above about 5 mg/dL.

q.q: Why do newborns develop physiologic jaundice?
o: High RBC mass with short RBC life and an immature liver
Bile duct obstruction from a congenital malformation
Rh incompatibility, which is present in every newborn
Low RBC mass with long RBC life and a mature liver
q.e: High RBC turnover + immature liver = physiologic jaundice.

q.q: Which is a pathologic cause of hyperbilirubinemia?
o: Normal feeding in the first week
q.e: Pathologic: Rh/ABO incompatibility, hemorrhage, infection, infant of a diabetic mother, galactosemia, hypothyroidism, breast-feeding.

q.q: Jaundice is pathologic if it appears:
q.e: Jaundice in the first 24 h is pathologic.

q.q: In a term infant, indirect bilirubin above what is pathologic?
q.e: Indirect >13 (term) or >15 (preterm).

q.q: A bilirubin rise of more than how much in 24 hours is pathologic?
q.e: Rising >5 mg/dL in 24 h is pathologic.

q.q: In a term infant, jaundice lasting longer than how long is pathologic?
q.e: >7 days (term) or >14 days (preterm).

q.q: What is kernicterus?
o: Unconjugated bilirubin deposited in the brain
Conjugated bilirubin deposited in the bowel
Yellowing limited to the whites of the eyes
Liver failure caused by bilirubin overload
q.e: Kernicterus → cerebral palsy and deafness.

q.q: Long-term effects of kernicterus include:
q.e: Kernicterus causes cerebral palsy and deafness.

q.q: How does phototherapy work?
o: Blue light makes bilirubin water-soluble for excretion
UV light kills the bacteria that produce bilirubin
Heat from the lamp speeds up the infant's liver
Light blocks red cells from breaking down at all
q.e: Blue light converts bilirubin to a water-soluble form.

q.q: A side effect of phototherapy the RT should watch for is:
q.e: Phototherapy increases water loss.

q.q: For dangerously high bilirubin levels, treatment is:
q.e: Exchange transfusion for high levels; also treat the cause.

q.q: What does TORCH stand for?
q.e: Toxoplasmosis · Other · Rubella · CMV · Herpes simplex.

q.q: Toxoplasmosis is acquired from:
q.e: Cat feces or raw meat; causes hydrocephalus, seizures, jaundice.

q.q: Congenital rubella classically causes:
q.e: Rubella triad: cataracts, heart defects, deafness.

q.q: Congenital rubella is prevented by:
q.e: Maternal vaccination prevents congenital rubella.

q.q: Which TORCH infection causes progressive hearing loss and microcephaly?
q.e: CMV: IUGR, liver damage, microcephaly, progressive hearing loss.

q.q: Herpes simplex type 2 is usually acquired:
q.e: HSV-2 is picked up from the birth canal.

q.q: Treatment for neonatal herpes is:
q.e: Antivirals (acyclovir); cesarean if active maternal lesions.

q.q: Which infection belongs in the 'Other' category of TORCH?
q.e: Other: syphilis, HIV, coxsackievirus, varicella, parvovirus B19.

q.q: Why are the TORCH infections grouped together?
o: They cross to the fetus and cause similar findings
They are all treated with ampicillin
q.e: They share findings: IUGR, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly.

q.q: An atrial septal defect results when:
o: The foramen-ovale flap fails to cover the opening
The ventricular septum fails to form
q.e: ASD = failure of the FO flap to close the opening.

q.q: After birth, blood flows across an ASD in which direction?
q.e: After birth LA pressure is higher, so flow is left-to-right.

q.q: The most common type of ASD is:
q.e: Ostium secundum is most common; often symptomless.

sections.title: Pediatric Resuscitation & Emergencies
sections.covers: PALS pulseless arrest — shockable and non-shockable rhythms · SIDS · pediatric vs adult anatomy · body surface area and burns · upper airway hazards

q.q: Which rhythms are shockable in pediatric pulseless arrest?
q.e: Shockable: VF and pulseless VT → defibrillate.

q.q: Which rhythms are non-shockable?
q.e: Non-shockable: asystole and PEA → CPR and epinephrine.

q.q: A pulseless child is in asystole. Treatment?
q.e: Asystole is non-shockable: CPR + epinephrine.

q.q: A pulseless child shows ventricular fibrillation. Treatment?
o: Give atropine and check for a pulse
q.e: VF is shockable: shock, then resume CPR immediately.

q.q: The monitor shows organized electrical activity but there is no pulse. This is:
q.e: Pulseless electrical activity — non-shockable.

q.q: How often is the rhythm rechecked during pediatric CPR?
q.e: Recheck every 2 minutes.

q.q: Compression rate in pediatric CPR is:
q.e: ≥100 compressions/min.

q.q: Compression depth in pediatric CPR is:
q.e: Depth = ⅓ of the chest.

q.q: Compression-to-ventilation ratio for a child who isn't intubated (per the deck)?
q.e: 30:2 if not intubated (deck). Once intubated: 1 breath every 6–8 s with continuous compressions.

q.q: Once a child is intubated during CPR, ventilate at:
q.e: 1 breath every 6–8 s if intubated (per the deck; current AHA PALS guidance is every 2–3 s).

q.q: If IV access can't be obtained quickly in pediatric arrest, use:
q.e: IV or IO access.

q.q: SIDS is:
o: Sudden unexplained death during sleep of an infant under 1 year
Sudden death from a known airway obstruction during sleep
Death of a newborn within the first 24 hours of life
Any apnea spell that resolves with gentle stimulation
q.e: Sudden, unexplained infant death under 1 year; diagnosed at autopsy.

q.q: How is SIDS diagnosed?
q.e: SIDS is a diagnosis made at autopsy.

q.q: SIDS most often occurs at what age?
q.e: Peak 2–4 months; winter, night, males > females.

q.q: Which is a major risk factor for SIDS?
q.e: Maternal smoking is a leading risk; also stomach sleeping, prematurity, soft bedding, bed sharing.

q.q: What sleep position is recommended to prevent SIDS?
q.e: 'Back to Sleep' — supine. Watch: the slide says prone; Whitaker says prone is the #1 risk. Ask your instructor which they accept.

q.q: Which is a SIDS prevention measure?
q.e: Back to Sleep, smoke-free home, firm bedding.

q.q: Which pattern fits SIDS?
o: Winter, at night, more often males
Any season, only in daytime naps
q.e: Winter, night, males more than females.

q.q: Compared with adults, the infant tongue is:
q.e: A large tongue easily obstructs the airway.

q.q: Infants are obligate:
q.e: Infants breathe through the nose, so nasal blockage is serious.

q.q: In infants, which muscle does most of the work of breathing?
q.e: Cartilaginous ribs and an unstable thorax leave the diaphragm doing the work.

q.q: Why can a foreign body in a child go to either mainstem bronchus?
o: The bronchi have less angle than an adult's
The trachea is wider than an adult's
The carina sits lower in the chest
The right bronchus is narrower and steeper
q.e: In children the mainstem angles are more similar, so aspiration can go either side.

q.q: About what percent of an infant's body is water?
q.e: About 80% water.

q.q: Compared with adults, children have:
o: A higher metabolic rate and O₂ need
A smaller BSA relative to size
q.e: Higher metabolic rate and O₂ demand; larger BSA; immature skin and BBB.

q.q: Which pediatric feature raises the risk of head injury?
o: A large head with less soft-tissue protection
A small head with a thick, rigid skull
A thick skull that resists fracture
Strong neck muscles that hold the head still
q.e: Large head, less soft-tissue protection.

q.q: A child's proportionately larger body surface area means:
q.e: Larger BSA → more heat loss, more water loss, larger %BSA per injury.

q.q: A child's head is about what percent of BSA at birth?
q.e: About 19% at birth vs about 8% in the adult — use an age-adjusted chart, not the adult Rule of Nines.

q.q: How is burn BSA estimated in children?
q.e: Rule of Nines is for adults; use an age-adjusted chart for children.

q.q: The Parkland formula is:
q.e: 4 mL × kg × %BSA; half in the first 8 hours.

q.q: A 20-kg child has 30% BSA burns. Total Parkland fluid for 24 h?
q.e: 4 × 20 × 30 = 2,400 mL; half (1,200 mL) in the first 8 h.

q.q: Under Parkland, how much of the fluid is given in the first 8 hours?
q.e: Half in the first 8 h, the rest over the next 16 h.

q.q: Epiglottitis is caused by:
q.e: Epiglottitis is bacterial (Hib), ages 2–6.

q.q: A 4-year-old has a high fever, drooling and sits leaning forward. Suspect:
q.e: Rapid onset, high fever, drooling, tripod posture = epiglottitis.

q.q: The thumb sign on a lateral neck x-ray indicates:
q.e: Thumb sign = swollen epiglottis.

q.q: Management of suspected epiglottitis is:
o: O₂, keep the child calm, intubate in the OR
Examine the throat with a tongue blade
Lay the child flat for an x-ray
q.e: Give O₂, keep calm, intubate in the OR. Don't provoke complete obstruction.

q.q: Croup is:
q.e: Viral, subglottic, ages 6 months–3 years.

q.q: A 2-year-old had a cold, now has a barky cough and stridor. Suspect:
q.e: Cold first, then barky cough and stridor = croup.

q.q: The steeple sign on x-ray indicates:
q.e: Steeple sign = subglottic narrowing in croup.

q.q: If croup worsens despite humidity and fluids, give:
q.e: Racemic epinephrine and steroids for worsening croup.

q.q: Sudden dry, hacking cough in a toddler with no illness suggests:
q.e: Foreign body: sudden onset. Diagnosed by x-ray, removed by bronchoscopy.

q.q: How is an aspirated foreign body removed?
q.e: Removed by bronchoscopy.

q.q: How is carbon monoxide poisoning diagnosed?
q.e: CO-oximetry measures COHb. Pulse ox reads falsely normal. Watch: the slide says CO₂ — the answer is carboxyhemoglobin.

q.q: Immediate treatment for smoke or CO inhalation is:
q.e: Immediate O₂; watch for airway damage.

q.q: A newborn turns pink when crying but cyanotic when quiet, and a catheter won't pass through the nose. Suspect:
q.e: Blocked nasal passages in an obligate nose breather; treat with an oral airway or intubation.

q.q: Pierre Robin sequence causes airway obstruction because:
o: The jaw is too small, so the tongue blocks the airway
The nasal passages are blocked by bone or tissue
The epiglottis is swollen from bacterial infection
The trachea is too soft and collapses on inspiration
q.e: Small jaw → tongue falls back and blocks the airway.

q.q: Pica is:
o: Refusing to eat to stay thin
Eating only one type of food
q.e: Pica: dirt, paint, hair.

q.q: A major risk of pica is:
q.e: Pica risks nutrient deficiency and lead poisoning.

q.q: Anorexia nervosa is:
o: Refusing to eat in pursuit of thinness
Eating non-food items like dirt or paint
q.e: Anorexia = refusal to eat to be thin.

q.q: Bulimia nervosa is:
q.e: Binge then purge (vomiting or laxatives).

q.q: Eroded tooth enamel in a teenager suggests:
q.e: Repeated vomiting erodes enamel — bulimia.

q.q: Anorexia and bulimia are most common in:
q.e: Most common in adolescent girls, with distorted body image and perfectionism.

q.q: Global developmental delay means delay in:
q.e: Global = 2+ areas delayed.

q.q: ADHD is classified as:
q.e: ADHD types: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined.

q.q: Asperger's is described as:
o: A motor delay with normal social skills
A sleep disorder with daytime fatigue
q.e: Asperger's = higher functioning, normal intelligence.

q.q: Chronic defiance and anger toward authority describes:
q.e: ODD = chronic defiance and anger.

q.q: Aggression, cruelty, destruction and stealing describe:
q.e: Conduct disorder.

q.q: Which areas are assessed in pediatric development?
o: Language, fine and gross motor, personal-social and cognitive
Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and temperature
Height, weight, head circumference and body mass index
Lung volumes, flows, diffusion and airway resistance
q.e: Developmental assessment covers language, motor, personal-social and cognitive, plus the neuro exam.

q.q: How are OSA and behavior problems related, per Whitaker?
o: Untreated OSA causes behavior and learning problems
Behavior problems cause the airway to obstruct at night
The two are unrelated and should be treated separately
OSA only affects growth and has no behavior effects
q.e: Watch: the slide shows behavior problems 'resulting in' OSA; the book says OSA causes them.

q.q: Obstructive apnea is:
q.e: Obstructive = effort without flow; central = no effort.

q.q: Central apnea differs from obstructive apnea because in central apnea:
q.e: Central apnea = no respiratory effort.

q.q: The main cause of pediatric OSA is:
q.e: Enlarged tonsils and adenoids, plus obesity, small jaw or large tongue.

q.q: How is OSA diagnosed?
q.e: Polysomnography.

q.q: The usual first treatment for pediatric OSA is:
q.e: T&A, or nasal CPAP during sleep.

q.q: If surgery isn't an option, pediatric OSA is treated with:
q.e: Nasal CPAP during sleep.

q.q: About what percent of children have OSA?
q.e: Affects 2–4% of children.

q.q: Which sign suggests OSA in a child?
q.e: Loud snoring, disrupted sleep, behavior and learning problems (can look like ADHD), bedwetting, poor growth, high BP.

q.q: Pediatric OSA can be mistaken for:
q.e: Its behavior and learning problems can look like ADHD.

q.q: Normal pH for neonates and children is:
q.e: Normal 7.35–7.45; acceptable 7.30–7.50.

q.q: A pH below 7.35 is:
q.e: Below 7.35 = acidemia; above 7.45 = alkalemia.

q.q: A pH above 7.45 is:
q.e: Above 7.45 = alkalemia.

q.q: A fetal scalp pH of 7.22 indicates:
q.e: >7.25 normal · 7.20–7.24 slight · <7.20 severe.

q.q: A normal fetal scalp pH is above:
q.e: Fetal scalp pH >7.25 = normal.

q.q: pH below 7.25 with PaCO₂ above 60 indicates:
q.e: pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ >60 = ventilatory failure.

q.q: What is the acceptable pH range in neonates and children?
q.e: Acceptable 7.30–7.50; normal 7.35–7.45.
